verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 1.2.16 (Southern recension as on itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 1.2.15 (offset because the CE drops Southern 1.2.12)
attribution_note: Valmiki speaking inwardly to himself is right. Minor reading difference: our Sanskrit opens 'tasyetthaṃ'; itihasa.io's Southern text reads 'tasyaivaṃ' (same sense).
translation_note: Faithful. 'Worry' is fine; itihasa renders cintā as anxious reflection, which a reading may prefer (he is thinking hard, not only fretting).
context: Valmiki has just watched a hunter kill the male of a pair of mating krauñca birds and, moved by the female's cry, has burst out with a curse on the hunter. Still looking at the bird, he turns inward and asks what it was that came out of him. In the next verses he thinks it through and tells his disciple the words have the form of a new metre, the śloka.

key_terms.sense: anxious reflection, a troubled turning-over in the mind
by one struck down with grief
what is this that has been uttered by me?

core_teaching: Even a self-controlled sage can speak out of grief, and the mature response is to stop and examine what was said rather than defend it. That pause is what turns a raw outburst into something he can understand and use.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka), on 1.2.40
commentaries.gist: Tilaka maps the episode onto rasa theory: the slain bird and its mate are the cause of the emotion, and the sage's anxious reflection in v.16 is counted as a passing (vyabhicāri) feeling within the larger grief that becomes karuṇa rasa.
Govindarāja insists the outburst was not whim or anger: it came from seeing a clear wrong (killing a creature in the act of mating) joined with tender compassion for the bereaved bird.

practical_reading: After words said in pain or anger, take a breath and ask honestly what came out and why, before either regretting it wholesale or justifying it. Strong feeling, examined, can become insight or creative work.
misreadings: Not a teaching that grief or compassion is wrong; the commentators treat his feeling as righteous.
Not a call to self-punishment after an outburst; the verse moves to reflection, not shame.
cautions: Context involves a violent killing of a bird and a curse; mild, but note for very sensitive readers.
speaks_to: having snapped or said something harsh in grief or shock
noticing your own reaction and wanting to understand it
creative people turning pain into work
not_for: someone who is being blamed for normal grief; it could read as 'you should not have reacted'
a reader looking for comfort for a fresh loss (the verse is about self-examination, not consolation)
research_note: No commentary block on itihasa.io is keyed to v.16 itself; the two commentary notes are from the adjacent verses and bear on it directly. Griffith (Book I canto 2) confirms the sequence.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 1.2.40; Baroda critical edition 1.2.39. Our number 1.2.36 does not match either text checked; in itihasa.io's Southern numbering 1.2.36 is Brahma's 'yāvat sthāsyanti girayaḥ' verse.
attribution_note: Speaker is not the narrator: in itihasa.io (and Griffith, Book I canto 2) the line is spoken by Valmiki's disciples, who keep chanting the verse and say to one another, astonished, that the grief has become a śloka. Suggest speaker 'Valmiki's disciples', listener 'one another'.
translation_note: Sense is right ('his grief became a shloka'), though the subject in Sanskrit is 'the grief' that, sung in four equal quarters and repeated, attained the state of a śloka. 'Repeated again and again' refers to the disciples' re-chanting (anuvyāharaṇāt), not Valmiki's.
context: After Brahma has visited, approved the new metre and told Valmiki to tell Rama's whole story, the disciples chant the krauñca verse over and over and marvel at it. This verse is their exclamation. Right after it, Valmiki resolves to compose the entire Ramayana in such verses.

key_terms.sense: grief has come to be a śloka (verse)
in four quarters of equal syllables
through being repeated again and again

core_teaching: A private grief, given form and shared through repetition, becomes something lasting that others can receive. The poem's own origin story says its compassion (karuṇa) is born from sorrow.

commentaries.gist: Tilaka gives a full rasa analysis: the grief (śoka) is the underlying emotion; through poetic universalisation and the disciples' repeated chanting, personal sorrow becomes the aesthetic experience of karuṇa rasa.

practical_reading: Teachers use this as the founding image of turning pain into something made: a song, a poem, a journal entry said aloud to others. Shaping and repeating grief can change how it sits in you.
misreadings: Not a claim that grief should be quickly converted into productivity.
Not 'grief is good'; the verse honours the sorrow that the poem grows from.
cautions: Gentle for grief, but 'sorrow can become something you make' may feel premature in the first days of a loss.
speaks_to: people writing, singing or creating after a loss
grief that has begun to settle and wants a form
creative block rooted in pain
not_for: very fresh, acute grief where making anything feels impossible
someone pressured to 'be productive' about loss
research_note: Only one commentator (Tilaka) is synthesised for this verse on itihasa.io. Reference and speaker both need correcting.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 1.21.21 (Southern recension, itihasa.io). Not in the Baroda critical edition: itihasa.io marks 1.21.19, 21 and 22 as Southern-only.
translation_note: Faithful. The Sanskrit adds that Vishvamitra 'approaches and entreats' you; 'for your son's welfare' (putrahitārthāya) is well rendered.
context: Vishvamitra has asked for young Ram to protect his sacrifice from demons, and Dasharatha, terrified, has refused and angered the sage. Vasishtha steps in, lists Vishvamitra's powers and says there is no reason for doubt. This verse is his clinching point; in the next verse Dasharatha, calmed, agrees to send Ram.

key_terms.sense: for the benefit of your son

core_teaching: The sage does not need Ram; Ram needs what the sage can give. A parent's fear can misread an opportunity for the child as a threat.

commentaries.gist: Reads the particle 'ca' as 'even though': though fully able to deal with the demons himself, Vishvamitra asks for Ram purely for the prince's good, implying he means to hand over his whole store of divine weapon-knowledge.

practical_reading: When a mentor, school or opportunity asks to take your child (or you) out of a safe place, ask whether the request is really for their growth. Letting go can be the protective act.
misreadings: Not a rule that parents should hand children to any authority who asks; the case rests on Vasishtha's trusted judgement of this particular sage.
Not dismissing a parent's fear as foolish.
cautions: For a parent whose child faces real danger (illness, war, an unsafe situation), this could feel like being told to stop worrying.
speaks_to: parents sending a child away to study, train or work
anxiety about letting someone you love take a risk
resisting a mentor's offer out of fear
not_for: a parent grieving a child who left and came to harm
situations of coercion or where the 'mentor' is untrustworthy
research_note: Southern-only verse (absent from the critical edition); worth noting if the app labels critical-edition status. Griffith's is a loose verse rendering, not a commentary; counted only as a cross-check. Cross-checked against Griffith's 1870-74 verse translation (archive.org/Project Gutenberg), which matches the content; it is a translation, not a commentary.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 1.33.8-9ab (Southern recension, itihasa.io), where it is part of a longer verse; Baroda critical edition 1.32.8-9. Our two lines straddle itihasa.io's verses 8 and 9.
attribution_note: King Kushanabha to his hundred daughters is right.
translation_note: Faithful. Note the immediately preceding line calls forbearance the ornament of women as well as men, and says what they showed, especially toward a god, is hard to do.
context: Kushanabha's hundred daughters refused the wind-god Vayu's demand that they become his, saying their father decides whom they marry; Vayu in anger entered their bodies and left them deformed. When they tell their father, he praises their forbearance in this panegyric, comforts them, and then looks for a suitable husband for them.

key_terms.sense: forbearance, patient endurance, forgiveness; also a name for the earth

core_teaching: Forbearance is praised as containing the fruit of every other virtue: generosity, truth, sacrifice, honour and dharma. The world itself is held up by people who can bear and not retaliate.

commentaries.gist: Forbearance is equated with charity, truth and the rest because it yields the fruit of all of those duties together.
Agrees with Tilaka and adds a pun: kṣamā also means the earth, so 'the world rests on kṣamā' plays on the earth that bears everything.

practical_reading: Commonly cited as a hymn to patience and forgiveness: not hitting back when wronged, and holding steady so that others can rely on you.
misreadings: Not an instruction that victims of assault or abuse should stay silent or forgive the abuser.
Forbearance here is not passivity; the daughters had already firmly refused Vayu.
cautions: The daughters were harmed by Vayu after refusing him; praising their forbearance can read as praising silent endurance of sexual violence. Use with great care or avoid in any plan touching abuse, harassment or trauma.
Should not be used to tell a woman to tolerate mistreatment.
speaks_to: everyday irritation and the urge to retaliate
holding back a harsh reply at work or home
someone who chose not to take revenge and wonders if that was weak
not_for: survivors of assault, abuse or harassment
anyone in an unsafe relationship
readers being pressured to 'forgive and forget' a serious wrong
research_note: Griffith (Book I canto 34) confirms context: Vayu struck the daughters after they refused him. Our setting says they 'refused to curse' Vayu; I did not find that detail stated in the passages read, only that they showed forbearance toward a god.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 1.44.12; Baroda critical edition 1.43.12. Our number 1.44.10 is two verses early against itihasa.io (in its numbering 1.44.10-11 are Brahma's lines about Amshuman and Dilipa failing).
translation_note: Faithful. 'The vow they could not keep' is supported by the preceding verses, which name Sagara's line, Amshuman and Dilipa. itihasa glosses paramasaṃmatam as esteemed by the highest.
context: Bhagiratha has brought the Ganga down and led her over the ashes of his 60,000 ancestors (Sagara's sons), freeing them. Brahma appears, tells him to perform the water rites for them, and praises him for completing what Sagara, Amshuman and Dilipa had tried and failed to do. Next he says this descent has earned Bhagiratha a great store of dharma.

key_terms.sense: the pledge carried through to its end, fulfilled
bull among men, best of men

core_teaching: A task that defeated several generations can be completed by the one who persists; the earlier efforts were not wasted but carried forward into his success.

commentaries.gist: Glosses samatikrāntā as 'crossed over', the vow brought through to completion.
Same gloss, and reads the fame as one esteemed by the greatest sages.

practical_reading: Used to honour long, multi-generation or long-delayed effort: finishing a family's unfinished task, a degree or project years in the making, or a cause many people worked on before you.
misreadings: Not a claim that earlier generations failed through weakness; the text treats their efforts with respect.
cautions: Ancestral rites for the dead are in the background; mild.
speaks_to: finishing something long and hard
carrying on a parent's or family's unfinished work
persistence after repeated failure
not_for: someone who has just failed and feels it is final (it celebrates success, may sting)
a reader burdened by family expectations they never chose
research_note: Commentary on this verse is a single short gloss shared by two commentators.

verified_ref: Spans Southern recension (itihasa.io) 1.53.11cd-12 (Baroda CE around 1.52.10-11, which pairs half-verses differently). Our id 1.53.9 sits two to three verses early against itihasa.io.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to King Vishvamitra is right.
translation_note: Faithful. Our Sanskrit reads 'na parityāgamayaṃ'; itihasa.io reads 'na parityāgam arheyaṃ' ('she does not deserve to be parted from me'), which our English already reflects. Small transcription issue in our Sanskrit.
context: King Vishvamitra, a guest at Vasishtha's hermitage, has seen the wish-granting cow Śabalā feed his whole army and asks for her, offering a hundred thousand cows. Vasishtha refuses, saying she is bound to him like fame to a self-mastered person and that his offerings, rites and learning depend on her. The king keeps raising the offer, then tries to take her by force.

key_terms.sense: the dappled wish-granting cow of Vasishtha
she ought not to be given up
from my side, from my presence

core_teaching: Some things cannot be priced because a whole way of life depends on them; no offer, however large, makes them tradeable.

commentaries.gist: Explains the next line's comparison: Śabalā is inseparable from Vasishtha just as fame born of learning and austerity never leaves a self-mastered person.
With Tilaka, lists the rites resting on Śabalā (offerings to gods and ancestors, daily fire rites, offerings to all beings) to show why she cannot be sold.
Explains how even Vedic learning depends on her: her milk gives the purity of mind and bodily vigour that study needs.

practical_reading: Applied to values, relationships, integrity or a vocation that someone offers money or status to buy: knowing what is not for sale.
misreadings: Not a general refusal to negotiate or share.
Not about stubbornly hoarding possessions; the cow sustains his duties to others.
cautions: Vishvamitra later uses force and Vasishtha's sons die in the fighting; keep that in view if building a plan around the episode.
speaks_to: pressure to compromise integrity for money or promotion
protecting something precious from a powerful person
boundaries with people who think everything has a price
not_for: someone who genuinely must sell a cherished thing to survive (could feel like judgement)
a reader in a real coercive situation where refusing is unsafe
research_note: Griffith Book I canto 53 confirms content (not for a hundred thousand or ten million, or heaps of silver).

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 1.63.11cd-12ab; Baroda critical edition about 1.62.11cd-12. Our id 1.63.9 is two to three verses early against itihasa.io.
translation_note: Two issues. (1) 'As if they were a single day and night' slightly misstates: the Sanskrit (ahorātrāpadeśena) says ten years passed under the guise of days and nights, i.e. unnoticed, as if just a day and night. Acceptable as a paraphrase. (2) 'This obstacle came and I did not see it' adds 'I did not see it'; the line says, as I was overcome by desire and delusion, this obstacle presented itself. The preceding half-line, missing from our verse, says this was all the gods' doing to rob him of his tapas.
context: Vishvamitra had been practising severe austerity at Pushkara when the nymph Menaka came to bathe nearby; he invited her to stay and ten years passed. Waking from it, he sees the gods' plot to rob his austerity and is filled with remorse. He then sends the frightened Menaka away gently and goes north to practise harder.

key_terms.sense: under the semblance of days and nights; unnoticed, as if one day
of one overpowered by desire and delusion

core_teaching: Absorption in desire can quietly swallow years; the turning point is recognising it honestly, taking ownership, and recommitting.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka), on 1.63.12-13
commentaries.gist: Vishvamitra spares Menaka because he sees the fault as his own (she stayed at his request), and by not cursing he shows he has kept his vow to conquer anger.
Has him say the offence is his alone, as one who had become a slave to desire; so he dismisses her with gentle words instead of punishing her.

practical_reading: Used for 'where did the time go' moments: years lost to a distraction, a habit or a relationship that pulled you off course, and the choice to own it and start again without blaming others.
misreadings: Not a warning against women or love as such; the commentators stress he blamed himself, not Menaka.
Not a call to self-hatred; he regrets and resumes his practice.
cautions: Sexual desire is the context; frame carefully. Avoid shaming language about lost years.
speaks_to: realising a habit or distraction has eaten months or years
regret over drifting from a goal
taking responsibility instead of blaming the tempter
not_for: someone grieving a relationship (could read as 'it was a waste')
readers prone to harsh self-criticism or depression about lost time
research_note: Our Sanskrit begins mid-verse (second half of itihasa 1.63.11). Griffith Book I canto 63 confirms the ten years and the gods' plot.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 1.64.16 + 1.64.17. Line 1 is 1.64.16 = Baroda critical edition 1.63.15 (last verse of CE sarga 63); line 2 is 1.64.17, Southern-only (not in the CE). Our id 1.64.15 is one verse early.
attribution_note: Our data marks it 'Narrator (Shatananda) to Ram'. That fits: Shatananda is telling Ram Vishvamitra's story (itihasa's translation addresses Rāma). The second line is Vishvamitra's own inner resolve, quoted.
translation_note: Faithful. 'In his anger he lost what his effort had earned' renders 'when his austerity was robbed through anger'. 'I will not speak' may be a total vow of silence (Govindarāja) or a vow against cursing speech (Tilaka, Śiromaṇi).
context: Indra sent the nymph Rambha to tempt Vishvamitra; seeing through it, the sage angrily cursed her to become stone, and then realised that his anger had cost him his austerity. Restless and unpeaceful, he resolves never again to give in to anger or speak, and then vows not even to breathe for a thousand years while he dries his body in tapas.

key_terms.sense: when his austerity had been taken away
and I will not speak in any way

core_teaching: Anger quietly undoes years of hard-won discipline, and as long as the senses are unmastered there is no peace. The response is a firm, concrete vow of restraint.

commentaries.gist: Takes 'I will not speak' as a vow against harsh or cursing speech, the kind that just cost him his tapas.
Agrees with Tilaka: the vow is to give up curse-like speech.
Reads it as total silence and even holding the breath, since passions like anger arise only when the breath moves.

practical_reading: After an angry outburst that cost you something, make a specific, keepable resolution about speech, such as not replying while angry.
misreadings: Not a call to suppress all emotion or never speak up.
His breath-holding vow is ascetic hyperbole, not advice.
cautions: The following verses describe extreme austerity (not breathing, drying up the body); do not present as a practice.
speaks_to: regret after losing your temper
seeing how anger undid long effort
wanting a concrete rule for speech
not_for: someone who suppresses anger to the point of harm, or is being silenced
a reader in an abusive relationship told to 'not speak'
research_note: Composite of two verses of different textual status; the second half is Southern-only. Griffith Book I canto 64 confirms the content.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 1.65.3 in both the Southern recension (itihasa.io) and the Baroda critical edition (1.64.3).
attribution_note: Shatananda narrating to Ram is right.
translation_note: Faithful.
context: Vishvamitra has taken a thousand-year vow of silence and fasting. When it ends and he is about to eat, Indra comes disguised as a brahmin and begs his food, and the sage gives it away without a word. Through all such tests anger does not get in, and soon after the gods acknowledge him a brahmarshi.

key_terms.sense: become like a block of wood: motionless, unmoved

core_teaching: Real mastery is not the absence of provocation but the absence of an opening for anger: shaken outwardly, inwardly undisturbed.

commentaries.gist: Glosses 'like wood' as standing still as a log, and 'antaram' as an opening: anger found no gap to enter.
Stresses that he bore every obstacle and provocation patiently.
Takes 'antaram' as the inner mind: anger never reached it.

practical_reading: A picture of growth after repeated failure: the same provocations still come, but they no longer get inside. Useful for anyone working on temper over a long time.
misreadings: Not praise of emotional numbness; 'like wood' describes stillness in austerity, not not caring.
Not a claim this is quick or easy; it follows two failures.
cautions: Ascetic extremes (thousand-year fast) are mythic; avoid suggesting deprivation.
speaks_to: long-term anger work
staying calm under repeated provocation
hope after relapses
not_for: someone already numb or dissociated who might take 'like wood' as an ideal

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 1.77.26cd-27; Baroda critical edition about 1.76.14-15 (the CE pairs half-verses differently). Our id 1.77.20 is several verses early against itihasa.io.
translation_note: Faithful in outline. Govindarāja reads the contrast more sharply: Ram's love had two sources (his father's choice, and her beauty and virtue), while Sita's love for him was twofold in intensity. Our 'in her heart he lived twice over' fits.
context: The last sarga of the Bala Kanda: after the weddings and Parashurama's challenge, the family returns to Ayodhya and Bharata leaves for his uncle's home. Valmiki closes the book with Ram and Sita's happy early years, saying their love grew by each other's qualities and that their hearts spoke to each other without words.

key_terms.sense: a wife chosen by his father
from her virtues and from the quality of her beauty
dwells, moves about, in the heart

core_teaching: A marriage begun by the elders' choice deepens as each comes to love the other's character; love is something that grows, not only something found.

commentaries.gist: Ram's love had two roots, respect for his father's choice and Sita's beauty and goodness; Sita's love was twice as intense, flowing simply from his being her husband; their hearts read each other's unspoken thoughts.
On the next line, says each heart understood the other directly, by its own heart.
Takes that mutual understanding as knowing by insight (buddhi).

practical_reading: Speaks to arranged and long marriages: love that keeps growing because you keep seeing who the other person is.
misreadings: Not an argument that arranged marriage is superior or that wives should love more than husbands.
Govindarāja's 'Sita loved twice as much' should not be turned into a gender prescription.
cautions: Readers know the later separation and Sita's ordeal; for someone in a painful marriage, an idealised picture may sting.
speaks_to: newly married couples, especially arranged marriages
renewing appreciation in a long marriage
love that grows over time
not_for: someone in an unhappy or coercive marriage
recent divorce or widowhood
a reader pressured into an arranged match
research_note: Griffith Book I canto 77 confirms the 'double' dwelling-in-the-heart line.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 2.1.10 (Southern recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 2.1.15.
translation_note: Faithful. The Sanskrit is in the present tense (a standing trait), which our past-tense English handles fine.
context: The Ayodhya Kanda opens with Bharata away at his uncle's and Dasharatha thinking of making Ram crown prince. Valmiki paints a long portrait of Ram's qualities to show why the king and people want him. This verse follows the line calling him free of envy and peerless, and precedes the one on remembering kindness and forgetting wrongs.

key_terms.sense: speaks gently first; opens with soft words

core_teaching: Inner calm shows in speech: open gently, and do not let another's harshness set the tone of your reply.

commentaries.gist: Ram mirrors Dasharatha's noble bearing like a lamp lit from a lamp, and never retorts even when spoken to harshly.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka), on the preceding verse
commentaries.gist: With Govindarāja, defines Ram's freedom from envy (anasūyaka) as never finding fault in others' good qualities, the trait this verse continues.

practical_reading: In arguments at home or work, speak first and softly, and when someone is harsh, decline to escalate. Calm speech is presented as a sign of inner steadiness, not weakness.
misreadings: Not a rule never to stand up for yourself or others; Ram acts firmly elsewhere.
Not about suppressing all disagreement.
cautions: For someone being verbally abused, 'do not answer back' could sound like advice to endure it.
speaks_to: a short temper in conversation
family or workplace friction
wanting to be someone who lowers the temperature
not_for: people in abusive relationships
someone who already over-accommodates and needs to assert themselves
research_note: Cross-checked against Griffith's 1870-74 verse translation (archive.org/Project Gutenberg), which matches the content; it is a translation, not a commentary.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 2.1.11 (Southern recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 2.1.16.
translation_note: Faithful. Govindarāja's reading 'kathaṃcit' (by any chance) supports 'however small'. 'A hundred' is read by Govindarāja as countless.
context: Part of the same opening portrait of Ram's virtues in Ayodhya Kanda sarga 1, just after the verse on gentle speech. It is followed by the picture of Ram spending even breaks from weapons practice in the company of elders rich in conduct and wisdom.

key_terms.sense: through self-possession, a mind under his own control

core_teaching: Gratitude should be quick and generous, grievance short-lived; this is possible because the person is master of his own mind.

commentaries.gist: Ram is pleased by a single benefit even if done by chance, and forgets a hundred, meaning countless, wrongs.
Glosses 'ātmavattā' as having an inner faculty that is under one's own control; that is what lets him let go of injuries.

practical_reading: Keep a long memory for kindness and a short one for slights: notice and thank small help, and stop rehearsing old grievances.
misreadings: Not 'forget abuse and stay in harm's way'; it is about not nursing grudges, not about ignoring danger.
Not a demand that a wronged person instantly forgive.
cautions: Could pressure someone hurt by serious betrayal or abuse to 'just let it go'.
speaks_to: holding on to small grudges
family resentments
practising gratitude
not_for: survivors of serious harm still processing it
someone told by an abuser to forget what happened

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.7.35; Baroda critical edition 2.7.30. Our number 2.7.27 is eight verses early against itihasa.io.
translation_note: Faithful. Tilaka specifies she sees no difference in the love she bears as a mother for the two.
context: Manthara, Kaikeyi's maid, sees Ayodhya decorated, learns Ram is to be crowned, and rushes to warn Kaikeyi that this spells ruin. Kaikeyi instead rejoices, gives Manthara a jewel and says she makes no distinction between Ram and Bharata. Only in the next sarga does Manthara work on her fears and envy.
core_teaching: Kaikeyi's first, natural response is generous joy; the later envy is not native to her but talked into her.

commentaries.gist: Her words mean she feels no difference in the affection that comes from motherhood between Ram and Bharata; Tilaka also says her repeated 'dear news' shows overflowing joy.
Agrees that the repetition in the previous verse expresses rapture, not a flaw in style.

practical_reading: Our first reactions are often more generous than the stories others later feed us; notice who is stoking comparison and return to your own first, kinder response.
misreadings: Not evidence that Kaikeyi is simply a villain; the text shows her good-hearted at first.
Not a claim that jealousy never arises on its own.
cautions: The reader knows what follows (Kaikeyi's demand and the exile); use as a 'before' picture, not an ending.
speaks_to: blended families and step-parenting
being glad for someone else's success
noticing influence from a friend or relative who stirs envy
not_for: someone grieving a relationship destroyed by a third party's manipulation (may feel too neat)

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.8.9; Baroda critical edition 2.8.3.
translation_note: Faithful ('kila' carries 'they say' / 'indeed'). Our Sanskrit matches.
context: Kaikeyi has rejoiced at the news and even rewarded Manthara. Manthara refuses the gift and begins her campaign: first she frightens Kaikeyi for Bharata, then here she paints Kausalya as the lucky one, and next she pictures Kaikeyi waiting on Kausalya with folded hands like a servant.

key_terms.sense: with the office of crown prince
under the Pushya star (an auspicious date)

core_teaching: The voice of envy works by counting another's blessings for you and casting you as the loser in comparison.

commentaries.gist: After stoking fear for Bharata, Manthara now deliberately kindles co-wife jealousy, picturing Kaikeyi standing before Kausalya like a servant.

practical_reading: Watch for the 'lucky them' voice, from others or inside your head, that turns someone else's good news into your loss.
misreadings: Not a teaching to admire; it is Manthara's manipulation, quoted as a warning.
Not proof that women or servants are schemers.
cautions: The verse is the speech of a manipulator; a reading must frame it as a warning, not counsel.
speaks_to: comparison on social media
a friend or relative who stirs jealousy
envy at a sibling's or colleague's milestone
not_for: a day meant to comfort; it is diagnostic, not consoling
someone who is the target of a manipulator and blames themselves
research_note: Only one commentator (Govindarāja) is synthesised for this verse.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 2.11.3 (Southern recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 2.10.15.
translation_note: Faithful. Our Sanskrit reads 'pratijñā' where itihasa.io reads 'pratijñāṃ' (accusative, needed by the grammar); fix the transcription.
context: Dasharatha finds Kaikeyi lying on the floor of the 'anger chamber' and begs to know what is wrong. Following Manthara's coaching, she says no one has wronged her but she has a wish, and demands he first swear to grant it. He laughs fondly, swears by Ram, and she then names the two boons: Bharata's coronation and Ram's exile.

key_terms.sense: make a solemn promise, swear an oath
what I have set my heart on

core_teaching: The trap is in the order: a binding promise demanded before the request is known. Love and pride in keeping one's word make the king easy to bind.

commentaries.gist: Kaikeyi is carrying out Manthara's instruction to bind the king by oath before naming her demand; she asks for an explicit sworn promise.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka), on the preceding verse
commentaries.gist: Reads her 'I have not been wronged' as denying any humiliation by a rival wife, which shows how carefully she frames the moment.

practical_reading: Don't commit before you know the ask, especially when emotions are high and someone you love is pushing for a yes.
misreadings: Not a lesson that promises don't matter; the epic takes Dasharatha's word seriously.
Not a general distrust of spouses or women.
cautions: Kaikeyi's demand leads to Ram's exile and Dasharatha's death; frame as a warning.
speaks_to: pressure to agree to something unspecified
people-pleasing
family or business negotiations
not_for: someone grieving a betrayal by a spouse (could feel blaming)

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.19.33; Baroda critical edition 2.16.59.
translation_note: Faithful. 'As if he stood beyond the world': Tilaka takes this as like a jīvanmukta, one liberated while living.
context: Ram has just accepted Kaikeyi's demand and promised to leave for the forest. As he walks out, Valmiki says the loss of the kingdom no more dimmed his radiance than waning dims the moon, and that no change of mind showed in him. Next he declines the royal umbrella and fans and sends off his retinue to go and tell his mother.

key_terms.sense: one who has gone beyond all worlds; a liberated sage

core_teaching: Composure in sudden loss: the outward fortune changes, the inner person does not.

commentaries.gist: Glosses the comparison as being like a jīvanmukta who has transcended all worlds; on the previous verse, losing the kingdom no more dims Ram than waning dims the moon's beauty.
With Tilaka, reads the moon image as the waning moon whose inherent loveliness is untouched.
Reads the variant 'like the night (that does not dim the moon)' instead of 'waning'.

practical_reading: After a sudden setback (losing a job, a promotion, a plan) it is possible to carry yourself without inner collapse; your worth was not in the thing taken.
misreadings: Not numbness or denial; the poem shows Ram grieving later.
Not a standard that any visible upset is failure.
cautions: Could make someone in fresh distress feel judged for being visibly shaken.
speaks_to: losing a job, title or expected inheritance
public humiliation or demotion
wanting to stay dignified through a reversal
not_for: acute grief over a death
a reader who feels they 'should' show no emotion

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.21.48, marked Southern-only (not in the Baroda critical edition).
translation_note: Close. 'Hold your sorrow gently in your heart' softens 'saṃdhāryatām', which itihasa renders as 'restrain your grief within your heart'; 'sādhu' = 'well'. Our version is a fair, kind rendering but slightly less firm than the Sanskrit.
context: Kausalya has begged Ram not to go, even threatening to fast to death, and Lakshman has urged rebellion. Ram answers that his father's word must be kept, compares himself to King Yayati who fell from heaven and rose again, and here asks her to restrain her grief, promising to return. Next he says all of them must abide by the father's command; this is eternal dharma.

key_terms.sense: let grief be held in, restrained

core_teaching: A son asks his mother to contain her grief because the separation has an end: he will keep his word and come back.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of all three commentators (Tilaka, Bhūṣaṇa, Śiromaṇi), on 2.21.47-48
commentaries.gist: Explain the Yayati comparison: as Yayati fell from heaven when his merit ran out and later rose again, Ram will return to Ayodhya once his vow is completed.

practical_reading: For partings with an end date (a child leaving for study, a posting abroad), name the return and the reason, and ask for steadiness rather than denial of sadness.
misreadings: Not 'grieving is wrong'.
Not a promise usable for a death; the return here is literal.
cautions: 'Do not grieve' can land badly on someone bereaved; this is about a temporary separation, not a death.
Kausalya's fears come true in part (Dasharatha dies); avoid implying all will be fine.
speaks_to: a parent seeing a child leave home
long-distance separation with a planned return
leaving for duty or work far away
not_for: bereavement, especially early grief
partings with no assured return
research_note: Southern-only verse. Only one shared commentary note (on the Yayati simile) bears on it.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.22.3-4, both marked Southern-only (not in the Baroda critical edition). Our id 2.22.2 points to a different verse in itihasa.io's numbering.
translation_note: Faithful. 'Real cheerfulness' renders 'harṣam uttamam'; Govindarāja specifies the joy is that of saving their father through keeping his truth. 'Without fuss' for 'niravyayam' is loose; itihasa gives 'without obstacle/without loss'.
context: Ram has come from Kausalya's rooms to find Lakshman furious and ready to fight. He tells him to curb his anger and grief and cancel the coronation preparations with the same zeal that went into making them. He goes on to say that the reversal is Destiny's doing, so neither Kaikeyi nor their father should be blamed.

key_terms.sense: throwing off the sense of insult

core_teaching: The injured party himself chooses steadiness: drop the sense of humiliation, turn the energy toward the next right task.

commentaries.gist: The anger is Lakshman's at their father, the grief is for Ram; the insult should be dropped because the exile is not due to any fault or an enemy's win, and the joy to take up is rescuing their father by keeping his truth.

practical_reading: When a setback feels like humiliation, set the insult aside and put the same energy you had for the old plan into the new one.
misreadings: Not a rule that the wronged must swallow anger; Ram chooses this for himself and speaks to his angry ally.
Not toxic positivity: 'joy' here has a concrete reason (honouring the father's word).
cautions: Telling a grieving or wronged reader to 'take up cheerfulness' can feel dismissive; frame as Ram's own choice.
speaks_to: a supporter or family member angrier than you are on your behalf
redirecting energy after a lost opportunity
letting go of a sense of being insulted
not_for: someone suffering real injustice who needs to name it
early grief
research_note: Southern-only. Only Govindarāja is synthesised.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.22.29, marked Southern-only (not in the Baroda critical edition).
translation_note: Mild overstatement of doubt: the Sanskrit flatly says the forest is the greater good ('vanavāso mahodayaḥ'); our 'may be the greater blessing' hedges. Also 'reversal of fortune' renders 'lakṣmyā viparyaye' (reversal of royal fortune); our Sanskrit has 'lakṣyā', a typo for 'lakṣmyā'.
context: Still calming Lakshman, Ram says he will take his vow with water he draws himself rather than coronation water. Then he says not to grieve: between kingship and forest life, the forest is the greater good. In the closing verse he says neither Kaikeyi nor their father should be suspected; they are driven by Destiny.

key_terms.sense: forest life is of great good, rich in fruit

core_teaching: A forced change of path can be the better one; refusing to suffer over the reversal opens a different, larger good.

commentaries.gist: Forest life is greater in fruit because it frees him from the cares of statecraft, fulfils his father's word, and accomplishes the gods' purpose.

practical_reading: After a door closes, look for what the other road offers instead of only what was lost: fewer burdens, a promise kept, a chance at different work.
misreadings: Not 'everything happens for the best' as a brush-off of real loss.
Not a reason to tell someone else their misfortune is a blessing.
cautions: Can sound dismissive if offered to someone whose loss is fresh or severe.
speaks_to: a career setback or rejected application
relocation or a forced move
plans upended by family decisions
not_for: bereavement
serious illness diagnoses
someone who needs their loss acknowledged first
research_note: Southern-only verse; one commentator synthesised.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.23.17; Baroda critical edition 2.20.12. Our number 2.23.9 is eight verses early against itihasa.io.
translation_note: Faithful. Our Sanskrit has 'vipatrārthaḥ'; itihasa.io reads 'vipannārthaḥ' (whose purpose is ruined). Fix the transcription.
context: Ram has just said the exile is Destiny's doing and no one is to blame. Lakshman, enraged, rejects this: only the faint-hearted follow fate, and heroes overpower it by effort. He goes on to threaten to show the world today what human might can do; Ram calms him and keeps to his decision.

key_terms.sense: does not sink, does not lose heart

core_teaching: Lakshman's case: one who can counter fate with effort does not collapse when fate goes against him. The epic voices this through an angry speaker and Ram does not adopt it here.

commentaries.gist: Even granting that the parents' decision is fate-driven, Lakshman says such fate should be disregarded; only a coward submits to it.
Agrees with Tilaka: self-respecting heroes overpower fate by human strength and never lose heart.

practical_reading: Taken on its own, it encourages answering bad luck with renewed effort instead of fatalism.
misreadings: Not the epic's final verdict: Ram rejects using force here and keeps his father's word.
Not a licence for anger or rebellion against elders.
Not a claim that anyone who suffers simply didn't try hard enough.
cautions: Spoken in rage just before Lakshman threatens violence; a reading must separate the teaching on effort from the urge to fight.
Can imply blame on people whose setbacks are beyond their control (illness, disability, systemic issues).
speaks_to: fatalism or giving up after a setback
students or job seekers after rejection
feeling stuck and wanting agency
not_for: chronic illness, disability or grief where effort cannot change the outcome
someone already blaming themselves for not trying hard enough

verified_ref: Composite in itihasa.io's Southern numbering: 2.24.23 + 2.24.24cd + 2.24.25ab (Baroda CE 2.21.19 for the first verse; the lines about the 'terrible grief' and 'the old king's welfare' are marked Southern-only). Our id 2.24.20 is three verses early.
translation_note: Faithful; it compresses three half-verses. 'Take care' renders 'apramattā tathā kuru' (act with vigilance).
context: Kausalya, desperate, wants to follow Ram to the forest. Ram tells her that a wife must not abandon her husband, that Bharata will look after her, and asks her to keep the old king from being destroyed by grief. The verses that follow (Southern-only) state at length that a wife's highest duty is serving her husband, and Ram ends by asking her to wait for his return with rites and worship.
core_teaching: Instead of adding his mother's departure to his father's loss, Ram gives her a task of care: keep watch over the grieving old man.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis (commentators unnamed for this note), on 2.24.22-24
commentaries.gist: Ram answers her fear about the co-wives by assuring her that righteous Bharata will attend on her, while she must guard the king from dying of grief once Ram has gone.
Ram also prescribes rites and worship for her so that idleness does not deepen her grief while she waits.

practical_reading: When a family is hit by a loss, giving the grieving a concrete way to care for each other can steady them. Look after the elder who is taking it hardest.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of the surrounding verses' claim that a wife's only duty is to serve her husband.
Not a denial of the mother's own grief.
cautions: Adjacent Southern-only verses (2.24.25-28) teach strict wifely service and Tilaka elaborates them; do not import that framing into a modern reading.
Dasharatha does die of grief soon after; avoid implying the caregiver could have prevented it.
speaks_to: adult children moving away while a parent is unwell
caring for a grieving parent or grandparent
someone who wants to help in a family crisis
not_for: someone who blames themselves for failing to save a grieving relative
readers sensitive to gender-role prescriptions
research_note: Composite verse spanning CE and Southern-only lines.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.25.3, marked Southern-only (not in the Baroda critical edition).
translation_note: Faithful. Our Sanskrit 'dharma' should be accusative 'dharmaṃ' (as itihasa.io has). 'Goodness' for dharma is acceptable for readers; 'the dharma you uphold' is closer.
context: Kausalya has accepted that she cannot hold Ram back. Controlling her tears, she performs protective rites and pours out a long blessing: go, come back soon, and may the dharma you keep protect you; then she invokes the gods of shrines, the sages, the seasons and more to guard him in the forest.

key_terms.sense: may dharma protect you on every side

core_teaching: The goodness a person keeps, gladly and steadily, becomes his own protection. A mother's blessing turns his life's discipline into a shield.

commentaries.gist: Reads the variant 'dhṛtyā' (with steadfastness) beside 'with love', and notes the active verb stresses that dharma itself directly guards Ram.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka), on the next verse
commentaries.gist: Takes the 'shrines' in the following blessing as temples of the gods where Ram has bowed; Govindarāja reads them as crossroad shrines.

practical_reading: A blessing to say over someone leaving home: may the good you live by keep you safe. It also reminds the traveller that integrity is a kind of protection.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that good people never suffer; Ram suffers greatly in the forest.
Not a transactional 'do good and nothing bad will happen'.
cautions: For someone whose good, careful child was harmed, the idea that dharma protects could hurt.
speaks_to: parents blessing a child leaving for study or work
farewells before a long journey
anyone wanting to bless a loved one in a hard season
not_for: bereaved parents
someone who feels their goodness 'failed' to protect them
research_note: Southern-only verse; our id 2.25.2 is one verse early against itihasa.io.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 2.29.2 (Southern recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 2.26.2.
translation_note: Faithful. 'Because my love for you goes first' renders 'tava snehapuraskṛtā', i.e. I who am led forward by love for you.
context: Ram has just described at length the dangers of the forest (wild beasts, thorns, hunger, cold) to persuade Sita to stay in Ayodhya. In tears, she answers that these faults are virtues to her, and then goes through them one by one, arguing that with him she will fear nothing.

key_terms.sense: led forward by love; with love placed first

core_teaching: Love changes how hardship is weighed: what is a danger alone becomes bearable, even good, when shared with the beloved.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka; the page attributes this gloss to Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa)
commentaries.gist: Because she is led on by love for Ram, every forest hardship turns into a virtue for her.
Reads the word as qualifying the hardships: in her beloved's company they feel as pleasant as cuckoo-song, sandal-paste and mountain breezes; he also reads her face as only slightly tearful.
Takes the word describing her as 'deeply attached to her husband' rather than 'tear-streaked'.

practical_reading: In relationships, facing difficulty together can be chosen and even welcomed: a move, a lean year, an illness, when the bond comes first.
misreadings: Not a claim that a partner must follow wherever the other goes; this is Sita's own argued decision.
Not romanticising danger or deprivation.
cautions: Readers know Sita's later abduction; avoid implying her choice 'caused' it.
speaks_to: couples facing a hard move, job loss or long illness together
choosing to stand by someone in difficulty
partners being 'protected' from a decision they want to share
not_for: someone staying in a harmful relationship out of love
a reader pressured to follow a partner against their own wishes
research_note: itihasa.io labels the Tilaka gloss here 'Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa (Tilaka)'; the Tilaka is elsewhere on the site attributed to Rāma Varmā. Attribution of the Tilaka is debated; I kept the site's wording.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.30.10; Baroda critical edition 2.27.9.
translation_note: Faithful. 'Hardship' renders 'tapas' (austerity).
context: Ram still refuses to take Sita. She grows sharper: in the previous verse she tells him he can be the obedient one to Bharata, for whose sake he has been passed over, and here insists he cannot leave without her; whether it is austerity, wilderness or heaven, it must be with him. She goes on to say walking behind him will be no more tiring than a pleasure-couch. Ram eventually agrees.

key_terms.term: tapo vā araṇyaṃ vā svargo vā
key_terms.sense: austerity, or the forest, or heaven

core_teaching: Shared life is not conditional on comfort: whatever the setting, the point is to be together.

commentaries.gist: Reads the previous verse as Sita's retort: Ram may be the one submissive to Bharata, for whose sake his coronation was stopped; she will share austerity, forest or heaven with Ram alone.

practical_reading: A vow-like line for partners: I don't want only the good parts with you; whatever comes, let it be together.
misreadings: Not 'a wife must follow her husband'; Sita overrules Ram here.
Not glorifying hardship for its own sake.
cautions: Context includes Sita's sharp words to Ram, which a reading should not omit if it describes her as merely devoted.
speaks_to: couples facing hardship
standing by a partner in crisis
claiming your place in a shared decision
not_for: someone in a controlling relationship
recently widowed readers (the 'with you' may wound)
research_note: Only Tilaka is synthesised for this verse. Our Sanskrit includes a stray verse number ('।।१०।') that should be cleaned.

verified_ref: Composite in itihasa.io's Southern numbering: 2.40.8 (Southern-only) + 2.40.9 (Baroda CE 2.35.8). The famous 'rāmaṃ daśarathaṃ viddhi' line is 2.40.9.
translation_note: Faithful. Our Sanskrit has 'saṃsiddhaṃ' as itihasa.io; Govindarāja takes it as 'ready to depart'.
context: Ram, Sita and Lakshman are about to mount Sumantra's chariot for the forest. Sumitra has just told Lakshman that the family's code is generosity, sacrifice and giving one's life in battle, so he must guard Ram even at the cost of his body. Then, saying 'go, go', she gives this blessing; next Sumantra urges Ram to start the fourteen years that very day.
core_teaching: A mother releases her son by relocating home for him: the people he serves will be his parents, the place he goes will be his home.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of all three commentators (Tilaka, Bhūṣaṇa, Śiromaṇi)
commentaries.gist: Plain sense: so that homesickness does not shake him, Lakshman should treat Ram as his father, Sita as his mother Sumitra, and the forest as Ayodhya.
Adds further readings, including a Vaishnava one: Dasharatha as Vishnu borne by Garuda, Janaka's daughter as Lakshmi, Ayodhya as unconquerable Vaikuntha. Śiromaṇi argues against this at length.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja and Śivasahāya, on 2.40.7
commentaries.gist: Sumitra cites the family code of giving one's life in battle to tell Lakshman he must protect Ram even at the cost of his own body.

practical_reading: For parents letting a child go: tell them where to find family and home in the new place. For the one leaving: home can be made wherever you are with people you serve and love.
misreadings: Not a call to cut ties with one's own parents.
The Vaishnava reading is one commentator's devotional layer, not the plain sense.
cautions: The previous verse speaks of laying down one's life to protect Ram; leave it out of comforting readings or frame carefully.
speaks_to: a child leaving for college, work or marriage
homesickness
parents blessing a departure
joining a new 'family' at work or in service
not_for: someone estranged from family who may hear 'replace your parents'
a grieving parent whose child left and did not return
research_note: Our note's claim that Govindaraja gives devotional readings (Rama as Vishnu, Sita as Lakshmi) is confirmed by itihasa.io's synthesis; I could not verify 'tradition counts it among the finest verses' from a source read.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.44.10; Baroda critical edition 2.39.10.
translation_note: Faithful. Our Sanskrit has 'dharmaghnaḥ'; itihasa.io reads 'gharmaghnaḥ' (dispeller of heat), which our English follows. Fix the transcription.
context: Ram has left and Kausalya is lamenting. Sumitra comforts her: Ram is not to be pitied; the sun will not scorch him, the forest breeze will serve him in every season, and here the moon will embrace him at night like a father. She goes on to recall his divine weapons and says Kausalya will see him return.

key_terms.sense: embracing him all round, like a father

core_teaching: Consolation through trust: the person you cannot reach is still held, here by the natural world itself.

commentaries.gist: Cites the Upanishadic idea that wind and sun act out of awe of the Lord: so the sun will not scorch Ram, and the moon embraces him like a father.
Notes the forest breeze will serve him tempered to the season, cool or warm as needed, part of nature's service to Ram.

practical_reading: For a parent worrying about a child far away: imagine the child held and cared for where they are, and let that ease the night.
misreadings: Not literal protection by the moon; it is poetic consolation.
Not a dismissal of the mother's worry.
cautions: Reassurance can feel hollow to a parent whose child is in real danger.
speaks_to: parents of children far away
missing someone at night
worry for a loved one travelling or posted abroad
not_for: bereaved parents
someone whose loved one is missing or in danger

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.44.21, marked Southern-only (not in the Baroda critical edition).
translation_note: Faithful. 'Confusion' for 'moha' is fine; 'delusion' is closer.
context: Sumitra continues consoling Kausalya: with Lakshman marching ahead of Ram as his guard, nothing is beyond Ram's reach. She declares with certainty that Kausalya will see him back, and next pictures him bowing at her feet like the rising moon.

key_terms.sense: you will surely see (a definite future)

core_teaching: A companion's firm reassurance: the separation will end; let go of grief and confusion.

commentaries.gist: Notes the verb form is a definite future, stressing the certainty of Ram's return; on the previous verse, Lakshman would never walk ahead as guard unless Ram were the Supreme Person.

practical_reading: How to sit with someone who is weeping: stay, name what is solid (he is protected, he will return), and say it with conviction.
misreadings: Not a rule that grief must be cast off quickly.
Not usable as a promise about someone who has died.
cautions: 'Let go of this grief' is risky for any bereaved reader; this is about a living person's temporary absence.
speaks_to: comforting a friend whose family member has gone away
separation from a child or spouse for a set time
co-wives / in-laws supporting each other
not_for: bereavement
uncertain outcomes (missing person, serious illness)
research_note: Southern-only verse; one commentator synthesised. Our id 2.44.17 is four verses early against itihasa.io.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.46.23; Baroda critical edition 2.41.21.
translation_note: Mostly right, but our English collapses the two halves. The Sanskrit says princes should free citizens even from sorrow of the citizens' own making, and must never yoke them to sorrow caused by the prince himself. All three commentators read 'ātmakṛtāt' as the citizens' self-caused trouble.
context: Crowds of townspeople have followed Ram to the Tamasa river and are sleeping under trees, refusing to go home. Ram tells Lakshman he does not want them to suffer for his sake. Before dawn they slip away, confusing the tracks, so the citizens will return to Ayodhya.

key_terms.sense: from sorrow of their own making
must not be yoked to sorrow caused by oneself

core_teaching: A leader's duty runs one way: lift people out of trouble, even trouble they made themselves, and never pull them into one's own.

commentaries.gist: With the other two, contrasts 'ātmakṛtāt' (sorrow from the citizens' own deeds) with 'ātmanā' (sorrow caused by the prince): a true prince rescues subjects from their own woes and inflicts none.
Same reading as Tilaka; the page states all three commentators agree.
Same reading as Tilaka and Govindarāja.

practical_reading: For managers, parents and anyone with responsibility: help people out of their messes, and don't make them carry your troubles out of loyalty to you.
misreadings: Not a reason to hide your struggles from people who love you.
Not paternalism that denies people agency.
cautions: Our note says 'atmakrita is best taken as suffering caused by the prince himself'; the commentators read it the other way (the citizens' own doing). Update the note.
speaks_to: leaders and managers
parents not wanting children to bear their burdens
people whose loyal friends are sacrificing for them
not_for: someone isolating themselves and refusing help (could reinforce it)
research_note: Commentary is one shared note attributed to all three commentators; counted as three only because the page says so.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.58.19, marked Southern-only (not in the Baroda critical edition).
attribution_note: Ram to Kausalya via Sumantra's report is right (Sumantra is relaying Ram's message to Dasharatha and Kausalya).
translation_note: Reasonable. The two pride words differ: Tilaka and Govindarāja read abhimāna as pride in being chief queen or noble birth, and māna as jealous pique toward co-wives. 'Show Kaikeyi the respect the king gives her' follows one reading of a hard phrase; Govindarāja reads 'treat the king and noble Kaikeyi alike', Kataka reads 'salute Kaikeyi'.
context: Sumantra has returned from leaving Ram at the Ganga and reports Ram's messages to the king and queens. Ram asks his mother to keep up the fire rites, serve the king, drop her pride toward the other queens and honour Kaikeyi, and to treat Bharata as king.
core_teaching: Ram, the one wronged, asks his mother to keep the household whole by setting aside both status-pride and resentment, even toward the co-wife who caused the exile.

commentaries.gist: Abhimāna is ego from being chief queen; māna is jealous pique toward co-wives. Reads the last phrase as 'honour Kaikeyi, whom the king follows', and notes Kataka's reading 'salute Kaikeyi'.
Same distinction of the two prides; construes the line as 'treat the king and noble Kaikeyi alike'.

practical_reading: In a family rift, someone has to drop status and grievance so the household can function; sometimes it is asked of the injured party.
misreadings: Not a rule that the wronged must defer to those who wronged them in every case.
Not a denial that Kaikeyi did wrong.
cautions: Asks a wronged woman to defer to the one who wronged her; avoid using with readers in abusive or toxic family situations.
Surrounding lines ask her to serve the king 'like a god'; do not import that.
speaks_to: joint families and in-law tensions
sibling or step-family rifts after a conflict
dropping ego to keep peace at home
not_for: readers suffering ongoing mistreatment from a family member
someone being pressured to reconcile with an abuser
research_note: Southern-only verse; our id 2.58.14 is five verses early against itihasa.io.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.62.14; Baroda critical edition 2.56.10.
translation_note: Faithful. 'I know what is right' renders 'jānāmi dharmam' (our Sanskrit has 'dharme'; itihasa.io 'dharmaṃ'). 'What I said' is softer than 'something unfitting was said by me' (kim api).
context: Kausalya, in grief, had bitterly reproached Dasharatha for exiling Ram. Seeing the king in anguish with folded hands, she is shaken, places his hands on her head and begs forgiveness. She says she knows he is truthful and that grief made her speak; the next verse is the famous line that grief destroys fortitude, learning, everything; there is no enemy like grief.

key_terms.sense: by me, struck with grief for my son

core_teaching: Grief can make even a wise person speak against what she knows; the remedy is to name it and repair the relationship.

commentaries.gist: Kausalya says she spoke rashly and improperly only because grief destroys both steadiness and the settled understanding of dharma that comes from learning.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka) and Govindarāja (Bhūṣaṇa), on the preceding verse
commentaries.gist: Differ on construing the previous line about a wife whom her husband has to placate; both frame her apology as restoring proper relation with the king.

practical_reading: After saying hurtful things in grief, apologise plainly: acknowledge the other's goodness and own that pain spoke. It also invites forgiveness for others who lash out while grieving.
misreadings: Not 'grieving people must not express anger'.
Not a claim that Kausalya's complaint was baseless.
cautions: The preceding verse frames wifely duty in strong terms; keep it out of a modern reading.
speaks_to: apologising after an argument during a family crisis
couples grieving together
understanding a grieving relative's harsh words
not_for: someone whose grief-anger is justified and who is being pushed to apologise
research_note: Direct commentary on this verse is Śiromaṇi's note covering 14-16; the second entry concerns the previous verse.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.62.15; Baroda critical edition 2.56.11.
translation_note: Faithful. 'Learning' renders śrutam (scriptural learning); Śiromaṇi takes it as the settled understanding of dharma that study gives.
context: Kausalya has just apologised to Dasharatha for her bitter words, saying grief for her son made her speak. She explains with this verse what grief does, and adds that a blow from an enemy can be borne but even a slight grief cannot. She notes Ram has been gone five nights that feel like five years; the king, consoled, falls asleep.

key_terms.sense: what one has learned, scriptural understanding
there is no enemy equal to grief

core_teaching: Grief can undo steadiness and even what one knows to be right; it is named here to explain, and excuse, words spoken in pain.

commentaries.gist: Kausalya pleads she spoke rashly and improperly only because grief wipes out both fortitude and the firm grasp of dharma gained from scripture.

practical_reading: Explains why grieving people say or do things unlike themselves, and why grace is owed to them, and to yourself. Also a reason to delay big decisions in fresh grief.
misreadings: Not a command to suppress grief; it describes grief's effects to excuse lapses.
Not a reason to treat grieving people as irrational in everything.
cautions: Calling grief 'an enemy' may feel harsh to someone who experiences grief as love; frame as describing its effects on judgement.
Spoken in a household where the king is about to die of grief.
speaks_to: having lashed out while grieving
understanding a grieving relative's anger
why decisions feel impossible after a loss
not_for: someone told their grief is a weakness
a reader who needs permission to grieve rather than a warning about it
research_note: Only Śiromaṇi is synthesised for this verse.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 2.63.7 (Southern recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 2.57.5.
translation_note: Faithful. itihasa.io's text reads 'na bāla' in the last quarter (likely a typo); ours 'sa bāla' fits the sense. Our Sanskrit includes a stray verse number '।७।।'.
context: Late at night, five or six days after Ram's departure, Dasharatha wakes and remembers a wrong from his youth. He begins by saying each person reaps the fruit of his own deeds, then this verse on rash action, then the parable of the man who cuts a mango grove to water flashy palāśa trees. He goes on to confess how, as a young prince proud of shooting by sound, he killed a hermit boy.

key_terms.sense: the weight or lightness of aims

core_teaching: Before acting, weigh how much is at stake, what it will lead to and what could go wrong; acting without this is childish, however grown one is.

commentaries.gist: Distinguishes the 'aims' (worldly goals) from the 'actions' (rites aimed at the next world): both need weighing before one begins.
Applies it to Dasharatha himself: indulging in the trivial sport of hunting led to the catastrophic loss of his son; the mango and palāśa parable follows.

practical_reading: Pause at the start: how big is this, where does it lead, what could go wrong? Useful for impulsive decisions, from money to words to risky fun.
misreadings: Not a claim that every misfortune is punishment for a careless act.
Not a counsel of paralysis; it is about weighing, not avoiding action.
cautions: Spoken by a dying man about killing a boy by mistake; the frame is heavy.
speaks_to: impulsive decision-making
young people tempted by thrill or showing off
planning a major step
not_for: someone grieving a death caused by an accident they feel responsible for (could intensify self-blame)
a reader already paralysed by overthinking

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.63.12; Baroda critical edition 2.57.8cd-9ab (split across two CE verses).
translation_note: Faithful. 'Out of ignorance' renders 'sammohāt' (through delusion).
context: Dasharatha has just recalled how, as a young prince famed as an archer who could hit by sound alone, he committed a sin. Here he says this sorrow is self-made, like poison a child swallows unknowingly. Next he compares himself to the man deluded by palāśa flowers, and then tells the full story of shooting the hermit boy at the river.
core_teaching: Owning the past: present suffering is traced honestly to one's own earlier act, done in ignorance rather than malice.

commentaries.gist: Glosses the 'renown' of the young archer as fame for shooting by sound; also reads a second sense, 'having heard the sound (of the boy's pitcher)'.
Agrees with Govindarāja on both senses of the phrase.

practical_reading: Taking responsibility for consequences of a past mistake, even an unintended one, without excuses; seeing that ignorance can still cause great harm.
misreadings: Not a teaching that every sorrow is self-caused; Dasharatha says this about his own case.
Not a reason to blame people for their misfortunes.
cautions: Concerns the accidental killing of a young man; heavy.
Can deepen guilt for someone who has caused harm by accident.
speaks_to: owning a past mistake
regret late in life
seeing consequences of youthful recklessness
not_for: someone who caused an accidental death or injury and is in acute guilt
readers being blamed for their illness or loss
research_note: Commentary on itihasa.io focuses on the preceding half-verse; nothing specific on the poison simile.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.64.10; Baroda critical edition 2.58.8.
attribution_note: Our data says the blind father speaks to Dasharatha, taken for his son: correct, but note this is quoted inside Dasharatha's own narration to Kausalya.
translation_note: Faithful. Our Sanskrit ends 'kathaṃ tvaṃ nābhibhāṣase'; itihasa.io reads 'kiṃ tvaṃ no nābhibhāṣase' (why do you not speak to us). Same sense.
context: Dasharatha, having shot the hermit boy and heard his dying words, carries the water pot to the boy's blind, aged parents. Hearing footsteps, the father thinks his son has returned late, begs him not to be angry if they have hurt him, and says this. Dasharatha then speaks in a faltering, terrified voice and confesses.

key_terms.sense: the refuge of those with no other refuge
the eyes of those without sight
our lives are bound to you

core_teaching: The depth of dependence and love between aged parents and a child; the pathos is that the son is already dead.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka), on 2.64.11
commentaries.gist: Explains Dasharatha's reply as spoken in a voice choked with emotion, without clear consonants.
Reads the same phrase as 'with indistinct syllables' and a variant meaning 'utterly terrified'.

practical_reading: Used by teachers to show the weight of care for aged parents and the gravity of harm done to a family's only support.
misreadings: Not a comforting verse; it is a moment of dramatic irony and grief.
cautions: Very painful: a parent speaking to a child who is already dead. Avoid for bereaved parents unless the plan is explicitly about lament.
The only commentary found concerns the next verse, not this one.
speaks_to: adult children who are their parents' main support
understanding caregiving dependence
lament and literature of grief
not_for: bereaved parents
anyone who has lost a child
readers who caused an accident
research_note: No commentary on itihasa.io addresses this verse directly; the two notes concern the next verse.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.64.23; Baroda critical edition 2.58.19.
attribution_note: The hermit father to Dasharatha is right (quoted in Dasharatha's narration).
translation_note: Faithful.
context: Dasharatha has confessed to the blind sage that he killed his son by mistake. Weeping, the sage says that if Dasharatha had not confessed, his head would have burst; a knowing killing of a forest ascetic by a warrior would topple even Indra. He then asks to be taken to his son's body and, after lamenting, curses Dasharatha to die grieving for a son.

key_terms.sense: if you had not told it yourself

core_teaching: Voluntary confession changes the consequences of a wrong: it does not erase them, but it saves the confessor from the worst.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of all three commentators
commentaries.gist: All gloss the verb as 'would split asunder'.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi), on the next verse
commentaries.gist: Notes the a-fortiori argument: if a knowing attack on a forest hermit would bring down even Indra, how much more a mortal king; so Dasharatha's unknowing act plus confession spared him instant ruin.

practical_reading: Owning up honestly, without being caught, changes what follows. Teachers use it for confession, apology and accountability.
misreadings: Not a claim that confession erases consequences; Dasharatha is still cursed and dies of grief.
Not literal: heads do not burst.
cautions: Embedded in the story of a killed boy and a curse of grief; heavy context.
Our 'line' ('you were spared') is fair but should not imply he escaped consequences.
speaks_to: deciding whether to confess a mistake
guilt and accountability
repairing trust after a wrong
not_for: someone grieving a child
a person coerced into confessing
research_note: Our id 2.64.19 is four verses early against itihasa.io.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.72.29; Baroda critical edition 2.66.23.
translation_note: Mostly right, but 'performed my father's last rites' takes one reading of 'saṃskṛtaḥ'. Tilaka reads it as 'given funeral rites by Ram'; Śiromaṇi as 'tended in his last illness'. Since Bharata thinks Ram was there, either works; 'cared for' is safer.
context: Bharata, summoned from his uncle's home, arrives in a strangely silent Ayodhya and finds his father absent from his mother's rooms. Kaikeyi tells him Dasharatha has died. He weeps, asks of what illness, and envies those who were with him; in his confusion he then imagines his father simply hasn't heard he has come. He does not yet know Ram is exiled.

key_terms.sense: while I had not yet come
tended / given rites by them in person

core_teaching: The grief of the one who was absent: not just the loss, but having missed the last days and the chance to care.

commentaries.gist: Takes 'saṃskṛtaḥ' as honoured with funeral rites by Ram.
Takes it as 'served during his final illness'; in the next verse Bharata, in denial, imagines his father just doesn't know he has arrived.

practical_reading: Names the particular pain of not being there when a parent died: living abroad, stuck at work, arriving too late.
misreadings: Not blame on the absent child.
cautions: Speaks directly to a parent's death; appropriate for grief plans but gentle handling needed.
Could intensify guilt for readers who missed a parent's death.
speaks_to: missing a parent's death or funeral
adult children living far from parents
grief mixed with guilt for absence
not_for: readers in acute guilt without a consoling frame around it
research_note: itihasa.io marks this verse Southern-only in the collation while giving it a CE match in the verse badge; the collation lists 2.72.25 as Southern-only and 26-30 as CE 2.66.20-24, so 2.72.29 = CE 2.66.23.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.72.31; Baroda critical edition 2.66.25.
attribution_note: Bharata, speaking to Kaikeyi, is right.
translation_note: Faithful. 'Gentle' renders 'sukhasparśaḥ' (pleasant to the touch). The verb is present tense ('who wipes me'), which heightens his denial.
context: Still not grasping the death, Bharata imagines his father would have bent down to smell his head had he known Bharata was there. Then he asks where that comforting hand is. Next he asks Kaikeyi to tell Ram, now his father and brother, that he has come, and only then learns of the exile.

key_terms.sense: the hand pleasant to the touch

core_teaching: Grief lives in small bodily memories: the hand that used to brush the dust off.

commentaries.gist: Glosses the verb as 'wipes clean'.
Same gloss as Tilaka.
Explains the unusual verb form grammatically; with the others reads the next line as 'tell Ram I have come'.

practical_reading: Gives permission to miss the small things: a parent's touch, a gesture, a voice. Used in grief writing to honour specific memories.
misreadings: Not a call to 'move on'; it is lament.
cautions: Directly about losing a father; tender but intense for fresh grief.
speaks_to: missing a parent's physical presence
grief triggered by small memories
sons and daughters after a father's death
not_for: someone with a painful or abusive relationship with a parent (idealised memory may jar)
research_note: Commentary is grammatical only; the emotional reading is the text's own.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.75.20; Baroda critical edition 2.69.13.
translation_note: Faithful. Our Sanskrit has 'akalmaṣam' and 'sthitāṃ'; itihasa.io reads 'akilbiṣam' and 'sthirāṃ' (steadfast). Same meaning.
context: Kausalya, grief-stricken, has bitterly told Bharata he now has the kingdom he wanted and should send her to Ram too. Bharata, with folded hands, protests that he knew nothing, and then swears a long series of oaths calling ruin on whoever consented to Ram's exile. Convinced, Kausalya embraces him.
core_teaching: When falsely blamed, appeal to what the other already knows of your love, and stand by your innocence.

commentaries.gist: Because another's inner innocence cannot be seen directly, Bharata turns to solemn oaths to make it credible; losing a scripture-guided mind is the gravest curse he calls down.
Agrees the oaths, though phrased generally, are aimed at Bharata himself.
Adds that from loss of wisdom all ruin follows, which is why that curse comes first.

practical_reading: For being wrongly blamed in a family crisis: answer the hurt person gently, remind them of the relationship, and be patient while they see the truth.
misreadings: Not a teaching to swear oaths; the oaths are Bharata's dramatic response.
cautions: Kausalya's accusation comes from grief; avoid making her the villain.
speaks_to: being blamed for a relative's wrongdoing
family conflict after a death
proving good faith
not_for: someone who actually did contribute to harm and wants absolution

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.77.23; Baroda critical edition 2.71.22.
translation_note: Our translation inserts the list of the three pairs (hunger and thirst, grief and confusion, old age and death) as if in the verse. The verse says only 'three pairs'; the list is Govindarāja's and Śiromaṇi's gloss. Our note already says so; the translation should mark it as a gloss (e.g. in brackets).
context: On the thirteenth day after the cremation, Bharata and Shatrughna collapse with grief at the pyre site while collecting the bones. Vasishtha tells Bharata the rites are unfinished and he must not delay, and then gives this teaching. Sumantra likewise raises Shatrughna and speaks of the birth and passing of all beings.

key_terms.sense: you should not be like this

core_teaching: Some conditions come to every creature without exception; since they cannot be avoided, the bereaved must rise and carry on with what remains to be done.

commentaries.gist: Names the three pairs: hunger and thirst, grief and delusion, old age and death.
Gives the same three pairs as Govindarāja.
Cites other readings: birth and death, pleasure and pain, gain and loss; and Kataka's citation of the six stages of being (arising, growing, decaying, perishing and so on).

practical_reading: In grief, remembering that loss and death come to everyone can ease the sense of being singled out, and help one return to necessary tasks.
misreadings: Not 'stop grieving'; Vasishtha is getting Bharata through the remaining rites.
Universality of death is not meant to minimise a particular loss.
cautions: 'You should not be like this' can feel dismissive in early grief; use after the first days or with framing.
Directly about a father's funeral rites.
speaks_to: the days after a funeral
feeling singled out by misfortune
needing to function for practical tasks while grieving
not_for: the first hours or days of bereavement
someone who needs their grief validated before being told to rise

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.82.12; Baroda critical edition 2.76.11.
attribution_note: Speaker Bharata is right, but the listener is Vasishtha, the family priest, who has just urged him (before the assembled ministers and people) to accept the throne. The 'you' in 'you ought to declare what is right' is singular, addressed to Vasishtha. Suggest listener 'Vasishtha, before the assembly'.
translation_note: Faithful. 'Speak what is right here' renders 'dharmaṃ vaktum ihārhasi' (you ought to declare the dharma here).
context: After the funeral rites, Vasishtha convenes the court and tells Bharata that his father gave him the kingdom and Ram has kept his word by leaving, so Bharata should rule. Bharata, weeping, refuses: Ram, the eldest and most virtuous, deserves it. He then resolves to go to the forest and bring Ram back.

key_terms.sense: the kingdom and I both belong to Ram
you ought to state what is right

core_teaching: Some gains are not one's to take, however lawfully offered; Bharata counts himself and the kingdom alike as Ram's.

commentaries.gist: A Śrīvaiṣṇava reading: both the kingdom and Bharata belong to Ram as his dependents; one possession cannot rule another unless the owner commissions it, so Vasishtha should state their true relation.
Reads the last phrase as Bharata asking Vasishtha to state the righteous means by which Ram himself may take up the kingdom.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka (attributed on this page to Nāgojī Bhaṭṭa), on 2.82.9
commentaries.gist: Calls Bharata dharma-knowing because he knows the rule that the eldest is crowned, and says he desires the duty of serving his elder brother.

practical_reading: Turning down a benefit that comes from someone else's wrong, even when it is offered legitimately: an inheritance, a promotion, a credit that belongs to another.
misreadings: Not a rule that younger siblings must always defer.
Not a rejection of responsibility; Bharata later rules as Ram's trustee.
cautions: Few; it is a strong moral moment. Avoid implying anyone who accepts an inheritance is a usurper.
speaks_to: sibling rivalry and inheritance disputes
being offered something that rightfully belongs to someone else
