integrity under institutional pressure
not_for: someone who needs to claim what is rightfully theirs and is being guilted out of it
research_note: itihasa.io labels the Tilaka on this page 'Nāgojī Bhaṭṭa's Tilaka', elsewhere 'Rāma Varmā'; attribution of the Tilaka is disputed.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 2.84.9 (Southern recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 2.78.8.
attribution_note: Guha to his people is right.
translation_note: Our Sanskrit reads 'yadi tuṣṭas tu' (if Bharata is well-disposed); itihasa.io's text reads 'yadā 'duṣṭas tu' (when he proves free of malice). Tilaka notes both readings. Our English 'in good faith' fits either.
context: Bharata's huge army reaches the Ganga at Shringaverapura on its way to find Ram. Guha, king of the Nishadas and Ram's friend, fears Bharata means Ram harm, posts five hundred boats each with a hundred armed young boatmen, and says the army may cross only if Bharata proves well-meaning. He then goes to meet Bharata with gifts to learn his intent.
core_teaching: Prudent loyalty: be ready to defend, but make the final judgement on what the other person actually intends, and go find out.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka (attributed on this page to Nāgojī Bhaṭṭa)
commentaries.gist: Guha warns his men against hasty battle: if Bharata is well-disposed to Ram (or, in the other reading, free of malice), the army crosses safely; otherwise the boatmen will attack from the boats.
Stationing the boats on the southern bank blocks any crossing without Guha's consent, while keeping them ready to ferry the army at once if Bharata proves loyal.
Notes the scale of preparation (a hundred boatmen on each of five hundred boats) and that Guha's gifts include silks, showing he approaches with courtesy.

practical_reading: When someone's arrival looks threatening, prepare sensibly but don't decide their intent for them; meet them, ask, and then act.
misreadings: Not a call to treat strangers as enemies.
Not naive trust either: Guha keeps his guard up.
cautions: Guha offers meat and fish to Bharata in the text; a vegetarian-household reading might want to skip that detail.
speaks_to: suspicion of a relative or colleague's motives
protecting someone you love
conflict de-escalation
not_for: someone in real danger from a person with a record of harm (could read as 'give them the benefit of the doubt')

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 2.97.4 (Southern recension, itihasa.io), marked Southern-only (not in the Baroda critical edition).
translation_note: Faithful. 'Food' renders 'bhakṣān' (eatables; Govindarāja: poisoned cakes).
context: At Chitrakoot, Lakshman sees Bharata's army approaching, assumes Bharata has come to kill them, and wants to fight. Ram replies that killing Bharata to win a kingdom would bring infamy after he promised to keep his father's word, and that any wealth gained by ruining kin or friends is poisoned food. He adds that he wants dharma, wealth, pleasure and even the earth only for his brothers' sake.
core_teaching: Gain bought by destroying family or friends is poison: it should be refused outright.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka), on 2.97.3
commentaries.gist: Explains the infamy Ram fears: people would say he broke his pledge to his father, killed Bharata and seized the kingdom the father had given Bharata.
Agrees on the infamy and likens wealth won by killing kin to cakes mixed with poison.

practical_reading: Refuse any inheritance, promotion or deal that requires breaking a family member or friend; the 'win' will poison you.
misreadings: Not a rule against ever pursuing a fair claim within a family.
Not a judgement on anyone who received an inheritance during a family dispute.
cautions: Few; mild violence implied in context (Lakshman wants to fight).
speaks_to: property and inheritance disputes
business partners or siblings in conflict
workplace politics where you could rise by undermining a colleague
not_for: someone already being exploited by family and needing to assert their rights
research_note: Southern-only verse.

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 2.97.7 (Southern recension, itihasa.io), marked Southern-only (not in the Baroda critical edition).
translation_note: Faithful. 'Indra's throne' renders 'śakratvam' (the state of being Indra).
context: Continuing his answer to Lakshman at Chitrakoot, Ram has just sworn by his weapon that he wants kingship only for his brothers' welfare. Here he says the earth is not hard for him to win, but he would not want even Indra's rank through wrong. Next he says any happiness without his brothers may burn to ash.
core_teaching: Restraint is meaningful because it is chosen from strength: Ram could take the kingdom and refuses because it would be wrong.

commentaries.gist: Ram disclaims the kingdom not from inability, since his valour could easily win the earth, but because he spurns even Indra's throne if tainted by wrong.
Same reading; on the next verse, Ram invokes fire to burn any joy not shared with his brothers.

practical_reading: When you have the power or opportunity to take something by cutting corners, the question is not 'can I' but 'is it right'.
misreadings: Not boasting; capability is mentioned to show the refusal is free.
Not a rejection of ambition as such.
cautions: Few.
speaks_to: temptation to win unfairly
ethical choices at work
holding power responsibly
not_for: someone powerless in their situation (the 'I could if I wished' framing may not fit)
research_note: Southern-only verse.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.97.14; Baroda critical edition 2.91.4.
translation_note: Faithful. Our Sanskrit ends 'yad viśaṅkase'; itihasa.io reads 'yo 'tra śaṅkase'. Same sense.
context: Ram has told Lakshman that Bharata has come at the right time to see them and would never wrong them even in thought. Here he asks when Bharata ever did Lakshman harm, or what new fear makes him suspect him. Next he forbids harsh words to Bharata: any unkindness to Bharata would be unkindness to Ram himself. Bharata indeed arrives in grief, seeking Ram's return.
core_teaching: Judge a person by their record, not by appearances or fear; suspicion without past cause wrongs the innocent.

commentaries.gist: Glosses Bharata's visit as timely and Ram's question as asking when Bharata ever did any past wrong; on the next verse, an offence against the Lord's devotee is felt by the Lord as against himself.

practical_reading: Before assuming the worst about someone, ask: what has this person actually done before? Check fear against history.
misreadings: Not 'never be cautious'; it concerns someone with a good record.
Not a claim that past behaviour guarantees future behaviour in every case.
cautions: For readers who have been harmed by someone previously trusted, the logic 'he never wronged you before' may feel naive.
speaks_to: suspicion within families
jealousy or mistrust between siblings
assuming bad intent at work
not_for: someone in a relationship with a person who has a history of harm
research_note: Only Govindarāja is synthesised. Our id 2.97.12 is two verses early against itihasa.io.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.100.18; Baroda critical edition 2.94.13.
translation_note: Faithful.
context: Bharata has reached Ram at Chitrakoot. Before hearing the news of their father's death, Ram embraces him and asks a long series of 'I hope...' (kaccit) questions on statecraft: honouring elders, waking early to plan, consulting well, starting good work promptly, choosing wise ministers, fair justice and more. This one is about how to take counsel.

key_terms.sense: does not run about the country (leak)

core_teaching: Good decisions need a small circle: alone you miss the other side, with too many you never agree and plans leak.

commentaries.gist: Deliberating alone fails to weigh pros and cons fairly; with too many, unanimity is impossible and counsel leaks.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi), on the preceding verse
commentaries.gist: Explains that the last watch of the night is when a king should think through how to achieve the state's aims, the habit this question builds on.

practical_reading: For big decisions, consult a few trusted people, not no one and not everyone, and keep plans private until they are ready.
misreadings: Not secrecy for its own sake or a licence to exclude stakeholders.
Not literally about government only.
cautions: Few; administrative in tone.
speaks_to: managers and founders
family decisions
people who either decide alone or crowd-source everything
not_for: someone in grief or crisis needing comfort (it is practical, not consoling)
research_note: Our id 2.100.16 is two verses early against itihasa.io.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.100.19; Baroda critical edition 2.94.14.
translation_note: Faithful, except our Sanskrit has the typo 'madodayam' for 'mahodayam'. Note: the vocative 'Rāghava' addresses Bharata (also a descendant of Raghu); our English rightly says Bharata.
context: Next in Ram's kaccit questions at Chitrakoot, after the one on taking counsel. It is followed by asking whether other kings learn of Bharata's undertakings only after they are done, and whether a single wise counsellor is preferred to a thousand fools.

key_terms.sense: you do not drag it out

core_teaching: Once you have decided on a worthwhile, low-cost task, begin it promptly; delay lets the opportunity's value drain away.

commentaries.gist: Glosses the phrase as small means, great fruit, and quotes a maxim that time drinks up the fruit of what is not done quickly.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi), on the next verse
commentaries.gist: Takes the kings who should learn of one's work only once it is done as subordinate regional rulers.

practical_reading: Against procrastination: if a small action will pay off well, do it now.
misreadings: Not 'act without thinking'; the verse requires deciding first (viniścitya).
cautions: Few.
speaks_to: procrastination
starting a small habit or task
leaders with too many pending decisions
not_for: someone burnt out or depressed who cannot start things (may feel like pressure)
research_note: Second commentary concerns the next verse.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.100.22; Baroda critical edition 2.94.17.
translation_note: Faithful. 'Crisis' renders 'arthakṛcchreṣu' (in difficulties concerning one's affairs). Our Sanskrit has 'kuryānniḥśreyasaṃ' (missing a ya) and 'arthakṛccheṣu' typo.
context: Among Ram's kaccit questions at Chitrakoot, after asking whether Bharata keeps his plans from being guessed. Here he asks if Bharata prefers one wise man to a thousand fools. Next he says even thousands of fools give a king no real help, while one capable minister can bring great prosperity.
core_teaching: Quality of counsel beats quantity: one wise adviser is worth more than a crowd of foolish ones, especially in hard times.

commentaries.gist: Explains the grammar: 'a thousand fools' is in the ablative with an implied 'setting aside', i.e. preferring one wise man over them.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Śivasahāya (Śiromaṇi), on the next verse
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'ayutāni' as tens of thousands: even that many fools are no help.

practical_reading: Seek one trusted, wise mentor or adviser over many loud opinions, particularly when things are going wrong.
misreadings: Not contempt for ordinary people; it is about whom a leader relies on for counsel.
cautions: 'Fools' language may feel harsh; paraphrase gently.
speaks_to: choosing mentors or advisers
decision-making under pressure
information overload from many opinions
not_for: a reader feeling stupid or inadequate
research_note: Commentary is mainly grammatical.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.100.59; Baroda critical edition 2.94.50. Our id 2.100.51 is eight verses early against itihasa.io.
translation_note: Faithful. 'Who governs for his own comfort' renders 'prītyartham anuśāsataḥ'; Govindarāja: one who rules for pleasure without examining right and wrong. itihasa.io reads 'asrāṇi' (tears; Tilaka notes it can also mean blood).
context: Late in Ram's kaccit questions, a cluster on justice: is an innocent man ever punished without examination by jurists, is a thief caught red-handed ever freed for a bribe, do ministers judge disputes between rich and poor without greed. This verse warns of the consequence. Next he asks whether Bharata honours the old, children and learned men with gifts, affection and gentle words.

key_terms.sense: of one who rules for his own pleasure

core_teaching: Injustice to the innocent, through careless or self-serving judgement, rebounds on the one in power and destroys what he holds dear.

commentaries.gist: The tears of the falsely accused destroy the sons and cattle of a king who rules for pleasure without investigating right and wrong; he also warns against punishing without examination by jurists or freeing a thief for a bribe.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka (attributed on this page to Nāgojī Bhaṭṭa)
commentaries.gist: Notes the word for tears (asram) can also mean blood.
Glosses the ideal ministers as free of greed for bribes when judging disputes between rich and poor.

practical_reading: Anyone with power over others (managers, parents, officials) must check accusations carefully; harming the innocent has real costs.
misreadings: Not a literal curse that misfortune proves someone was unjust.
Not a reason to tell a bereaved parent their loss is punishment.
cautions: Speaks of the death of sons as consequence; keep away from grief plans or readers who have lost children.
Could feed a 'my loss is punishment' belief.
speaks_to: people who judge others at work, in schools or families
someone falsely accused (validation)
fairness and due process
not_for: bereaved parents
anyone prone to seeing their misfortune as punishment

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.104.17; Baroda critical edition 2.97.17. Our id 2.101.14 is wrong by three sargas against both texts checked.
translation_note: Faithful. Śiromaṇi reads 'out of immaturity' (bālyāt) as 'not knowing your mother's real intention'. Our Sanskrit 'jananī' should be accusative 'jananīṃ'.
context: At Chitrakoot, Bharata has begged Ram to return and rule, then again clasped his feet in tears. Ram embraces him and says a man like him could never sin for a kingdom; he sees no fault in Bharata and tells him not to revile his mother. He goes on to say elders have authority over wives and children, and that he will keep their father's word.

key_terms.sense: out of youthful immaturity / not understanding

core_teaching: The one most wronged releases the innocent from inherited guilt and asks him not to condemn his mother in youthful anger.

commentaries.gist: Bharata's being called Kaikeyi's son hints his plight comes from his mother's fault; by clasping Ram's feet again he makes full self-surrender; the 'sin' Ram rules out is hostility to an elder brother.
Glosses 'out of immaturity' as not knowing his mother's true intention.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka (attributed on this page to Nāgojī Bhaṭṭa), on 2.104.16
commentaries.gist: Takes the 'sin' as breaking their father's command.

practical_reading: Don't carry guilt for what a parent did; and be slow to condemn a parent outright, especially in the first heat of anger.
misreadings: Not a demand to excuse a parent's serious wrongdoing.
The next verse grants elders authority over wives and sons; do not import that.
cautions: For someone with an abusive parent, 'don't revile your mother' could feel like silencing.
Next verse asserts elders' authority over wives and children; avoid quoting it uncritically.
speaks_to: adult children ashamed of a parent's actions
siblings caught in parental conflict
releasing someone from blame that isn't theirs
not_for: survivors of parental abuse
someone being told to stay silent about family harm
research_note: Located by searching the Sanskrit across itihasa.io sargas 2.99-2.107; it is not in 2.101 in itihasa.io's numbering.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.102.13; Baroda critical edition 2.95.17. Our id 2.103.10 is in the wrong sarga against both texts checked.
translation_note: Faithful. Govindarāja and Tilaka take 'suvṛttam' as 'having carried out (his) commands well'; Śiromaṇi takes 'sāntvayan' as gently instructing. 'Comfort' is acceptable; 'praise' or 'encourage' would also fit.
context: At Chitrakoot, Bharata has told Ram that their father died grieving for him. Ram collapses and laments: what will he do in Ayodhya now, who will guide him once his exile ends, and who will speak those sweet words his father said when he did well. He then turns, grief-stricken, to Sita with the news, and they go to the river to offer water to the dead king.

key_terms.sense: well-conducted; having done one's duty well
from where (from whom) will I hear

core_teaching: Grief for a parent includes losing the one voice that recognised you when you did well; even Ram grieves openly before he consoles anyone.

commentaries.gist: Glosses 'suvṛtta' as one of good conduct in carrying out commands, and reads 'from whom' (which man) will I hear such words.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka (attributed on this page to Nāgojī Bhaṭṭa)
commentaries.gist: Same gloss of 'suvṛtta' as good performance of an assigned duty.
Takes 'sāntvayan' as gently instructing, so the father's words were both praise and guidance.

practical_reading: Names the loss of a parent's approval and encouragement, the 'well done' that no one else can give in the same way. It permits grief that is about being seen.
misreadings: Not a sign of weakness in Ram; the epic shows the ideal man grieving.
Not about seeking approval in general.
cautions: Directly about a father's death; tender for fresh grief but suitable for a 'see' day.
For someone whose parent never praised them, this may hurt differently.
speaks_to: grieving a father or mother
missing a parent's encouragement at milestones
adult children achieving something after a parent's death
not_for: readers with estranged or harsh parents
someone not yet ready to name their loss
research_note: Located in itihasa.io sarga 2.102, not 2.103.

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.105.16; Baroda critical edition 2.98.16.
translation_note: Faithful.
context: Bharata, at Chitrakoot, has again pleaded with Ram to return. Ram consoles him with a long teaching: no one is master of himself, destiny drags people from world to world, and here, that every gathering, rise and union ends. He follows with images of ripe fruit falling and a strong house collapsing with age, and concludes that Bharata should not grieve for their father but rule.

key_terms.sense: all heights end in a fall

core_teaching: Everything that comes together comes apart; seeing this clearly is meant to loosen the grip of grief, not to cheapen what is lost.

commentaries.gist: Ram uses this to remove grief over Dasharatha's death: hoards end in depletion, even the high stations of Brahma and Indra end in a fall, unions end in parting, life in death.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Rāma Varmā (Tilaka), on 2.105.15
commentaries.gist: Reads the preceding 'kṛtānta' (destiny) as Time: the soul has no independent agency, which is why Ram absolves Kaikeyi and Dasharatha.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka and Govindarāja, on 2.105.17-18
commentaries.gist: The following images (ripe fruit that can only fall, a stout-pillared house that collapses with age) illustrate that the only certain peril for the born is death.

practical_reading: In grief, the reminder that all meetings end can soften resistance and shift attention to living well now; in success, it guards against pride.
misreadings: Not 'nothing matters' or 'don't love'.
Not a reason to tell the newly bereaved to stop grieving.
cautions: Mentions death directly; offered by Ram after he himself wept. For fresh grief, may feel cold unless framed with that.
Govindarāja says Ram uses it to 'remove grief'; a reading should not instruct the reader to stop grieving.
speaks_to: grief after some time has passed
loss of status, wealth or a relationship
pride in success
anxiety about change
not_for: the first days after a death
someone who needs their grief witnessed rather than explained
research_note: I could not verify from a source read the note's claim that this is a widely repeated subhāṣita (it is commonly quoted, but no page I read says so).

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.105.24; Baroda critical edition 2.98.23.
translation_note: Faithful. Our Sanskrit reads 'astamite 'hani' (when the day has ended); itihasa.io reads 'astamite ravau' (when the sun has set). Same sense.
context: Further in Ram's consolation of Bharata: nights that pass never return, days and nights dry up lifespans, death walks and sits with every creature, and when wrinkles and white hair come no one can resist. Here, people cheer sunrise and sunset without noticing their own life wearing away; next, they welcome each new season while the seasons' turning wears away their breath.
core_teaching: Daily life's small joys mask the steady passing of one's own life; awareness of this is meant to turn attention to one's own conduct.

commentaries.gist: People rejoice at sunrise because it is time to earn and at sunset because it is time for pleasure, blind to life draining away like water from a cracked pot.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja and Tilaka, on 2.105.21-22
commentaries.gist: Urge Bharata to reflect on his own hereafter rather than mourn, since life ebbs whether one stands or walks.
Reads 'death goes with him and returns with him' in terms of the soul's journey short of final liberation.

practical_reading: A nudge to notice time: the days that feel ordinary are the life we have, so spend them on what matters.
misreadings: Not a call to stop enjoying ordinary pleasures.
Not 'grieve for yourself instead of the dead' as a rebuke to mourners.
cautions: Mortality-focused; heavy for readers with health anxiety or depression.
Our note's 'grieve for yourself more than the departed' follows the commentators, but can feel dismissive to mourners.
speaks_to: drifting through busy routines
birthdays and new year reflections
midlife reassessment
not_for: readers with health anxiety or recent terminal diagnosis
depressed readers who already feel time slipping

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.105.26-27; Baroda critical edition 2.98.25-26. Our id 2.105.23 is three verses early against itihasa.io.
translation_note: Faithful. Our Sanskrit has 'vasūni' (riches) where itihasa.io reads 'dhanāni'; same sense. Tilaka reads the image as two ships rather than two pieces of wood.
context: Continuing his consolation, Ram has said the turning seasons wear away life. Here he uses the image of two logs meeting on the ocean and drifting apart. Next he says no creature stays with loved ones at will, so the mourner cannot bring back the dead; then he likens every mortal to someone telling a passing caravan 'I will follow you too'.
core_teaching: Family, relatives and wealth come together for a time, like driftwood, and their parting is certain; this is offered to steady the grieving, not to belittle love.

commentaries.gist: Reads the image as two ships meeting on the ocean; as they part, so wives, sons, kin and riches separate.
Driftwood that meets and parts; on the next verse, no one stays with loved ones at will, so the mourner cannot recall the dead.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Govindarāja and Śiromaṇi, on 2.105.29-30
commentaries.gist: Every mortal walks the same ancestral road, like one telling a passing caravan 'I will follow you'.

practical_reading: Helps hold relationships lightly and gratefully: treasure the time together, knowing all meetings are for a while.
misreadings: Not 'relationships don't matter' or a reason for detachment from family.
Not a justification for abandoning people.
cautions: Could feel cold to a fresh mourner or to someone recently separated or divorced.
Lists wives and sons among things that part; sensitive for bereaved spouses or parents.
speaks_to: families scattering (children moving away, relocation)
friendships that faded
grief some time after a loss
not_for: very fresh bereavement
someone grieving a child or spouse in the early months

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 2.109.4 (Southern recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 2.101.4.
translation_note: Faithful. 'Merely boastful' renders 'puruṣamāninam' (one who only fancies himself a man).
context: At Chitrakoot the priest Jabali has argued, in materialist terms, that duties to a dead father are meaningless and Ram should take the throne. Ram replies that such advice wears the look of reason but is wrong; one who abandons moral bounds gains no honour among the good, and conduct alone shows whether a person is noble, brave or pure. He goes on to say that if he broke his word he would be ignoble while seeming noble.

key_terms.sense: one who only thinks himself a man / a hero

core_teaching: Birth, claims and appearances prove nothing; character is shown only in conduct.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka (attributed on this page to Nāgojī Bhaṭṭa)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'conduct' as Vedic conduct: it alone shows high birth, valour or purity; the deviant doctrine in the prior verse refers to materialist (Lokāyata) teaching.
Ram is establishing the Vedic standpoint against Jabali; vv. 5-7 form one condition: if he abandoned dharma he would be ignoble while seeming noble.
Abandoning the Vedic bounds would bring general confusion of order.

practical_reading: Judge yourself and others by what is done, not by family, title or talk. Integrity is visible in action.
misreadings: The commentators read 'conduct' as Vedic dharma specifically; a modern reading should not claim the verse rejects caste or birth outright, though it does put conduct above birth as evidence.
Not a licence to judge others harshly.
cautions: Commentaries frame Jabali's view as heterodox; avoid making a reading that belittles sceptics.
speaks_to: people judged by family background
young people building a reputation
integrity at work
resisting pressure to cut moral corners
not_for: someone already crushed by self-judgement over a lapse

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.109.9; Baroda critical edition 2.101.9.
translation_note: Faithful. Our English supplies 'if I live by desire'; the Sanskrit says this whole world would act by whim, the condition coming from the previous verse (if Ram broke his pledge). Our Sanskrit 'anvayaṃ' vs itihasa.io 'tv ayaṃ' is a transcription slip.
context: Ram continues answering Jabali: if he lived by this pledge-breaking path, to whom could he teach right conduct and how could he reach heaven? Here, the world would then act on whim, because people follow their kings. Next he says truth with compassion is the eternal conduct of kings; kingship is founded on truth and the world rests on truth.
core_teaching: Leaders set the pattern: if those at the top break their word for gain, everyone below learns to do the same.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka (attributed on this page to Nāgojī Bhaṭṭa)
commentaries.gist: If the king became self-willed, the whole world would follow; reads the previous verse as 'whose ancestral conduct could I follow?'
No discerning person would respect one who corrupts the world; on the next verse, royal conduct rooted in compassion is truth itself.
Shrinking from a liar as from a serpent shows that falsehood is the root of all wrongs.

practical_reading: Parents, managers and anyone others look up to: your behaviour is the real instruction. Keeping your word teaches more than any rule.
misreadings: Not a claim that subjects bear no responsibility for their own conduct.
cautions: Few.
speaks_to: parents modelling behaviour
managers and team leads
public figures and teachers
not_for: someone blaming themselves for a child's or employee's choices entirely

verified_ref: Valmiki Ramayana 2.112.19 (Southern recension, itihasa.io); Baroda critical edition 2.104.19.
translation_note: Minor: 'from desire or greed' takes kāma as desire; Govindarāja reads 'kāmāt' as 'out of affection (sneha)' for Bharata, which makes the line gentler: whether she did it from love for you or from greed. Our 'line' ('out of wanting or greed') is fine; the translation could say 'love or greed'.
context: At the end of the Chitrakoot meeting, Ram has sworn that the moon may lose its light or the Himalaya its snow, but he will not break his father's promise. He then asks Bharata not to hold Kaikeyi's act against her and to treat her as his mother. Bharata, prompted by Vasishtha, asks Ram to step onto the golden sandals, which he takes back to rule in Ram's name.

key_terms.sense: whether from affection/desire or from greed
this was done for your sake
do not keep it in mind

core_teaching: Ram, the one most wronged, asks Bharata to release resentment and keep treating Kaikeyi as his mother, whatever her motive.

commentaries.gist: Anticipating the argument that a promise made under passion can be dropped, Ram says whether Kaikeyi acted from affection or greed, Bharata must not resent her and must treat her as a mother.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka (attributed on this page to Nāgojī Bhaṭṭa)
commentaries.gist: Finds a pun: 'by the mother' can also be read as 'by the gods', who engineered the exile through Manthara, shifting blame off Kaikeyi.

practical_reading: Letting go of resentment toward a parent whose choices hurt the family, without pretending they were right.
misreadings: Not a demand to deny the harm or restore full trust immediately.
Tilaka's 'the gods did it' reading is one commentator's pun, not the plain sense.
cautions: Not suitable for readers harmed by a parent's abuse or neglect; 'treat her as your mother still' may feel like a demand to reconcile.
Sensitive in blended families where step-parents caused harm.
speaks_to: anger at a parent's decision that hurt a sibling
family rifts over inheritance or favouritism
choosing not to carry resentment
not_for: survivors of parental abuse
someone pressured into reconciliation

verified_ref: Southern recension (itihasa.io) 2.115.17: first line Southern-only, second line = Baroda critical edition 2.107.14.
attribution_note: Bharata speaking at Nandigrama is right; itihasa.io's context has him addressing the assembled people and ministers (he tells them to hold the royal umbrella over the sandals). 'Advisers' is acceptable.
translation_note: Faithful. 'This' = 'saṃnyāsaḥ', a deposit placed in trust; Govindarāja stresses it must be returned undiminished.
context: Bharata has returned from Chitrakoot with Ram's sandals. Rather than enter Ayodhya, he settles at Nandigrama in ascetic dress, installs the sandals on the throne, and has the royal umbrella held over them, saying dharma stands in the kingdom through them. Here he says the kingdom is a trust he will guard until Ram returns; next he vows to put the sandals back on Ram's feet with his own hands.
core_teaching: Power held as a trust: Bharata rules not as owner but as guardian of what was entrusted to him in love, to be returned intact.

commentaries.gist: Fearing talk that he rules a kingdom won by his mother's boon, Bharata calls it a sacred deposit that must be returned intact; he has no independent authority, the sandals bear its welfare.

commentaries.who: itihasa.io synthesis of Tilaka (attributed on this page to Nāgojī Bhaṭṭa)
commentaries.gist: Defines a deposit (nyāsa) as property left with a trusted person to be reclaimed later; through the sandals Bharata gains knowledge of dharma in every dealing.
Bharata vows to guard and serve this sacred trust until Ram returns.

practical_reading: For anyone holding a role, money or responsibility on someone else's behalf (a caretaker, interim leader, guardian): treat it as a trust to be returned in good order.
misreadings: Not a call to self-denial for its own sake; Bharata's austerity is his choice.
Not about refusing all responsibility.
cautions: Few.
speaks_to: interim or acting roles
caring for a family business or home while someone is away
guardianship and stewardship
not_for: someone resentful about carrying another's burden without recognition (may feel like being told to accept it)
research_note: Composite of a Southern-only line and a CE line.
